article.title: Regression to the Mean: Why Extreme Customers Often Look More Normal Later
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: A company identifies its highest-spending customers and notices that their spending falls the following year. Another team targets the least active users and later observes that their activity improves. Both teams may be tempted to attribute the change to a business intervention. Yet part of the movement can occur even when nothing causal happened. This phenomenon is regression to the mean. Observed behavior combines relatively persistent characteristics with temporary variation. A customer may spend unusually much because of a large one-time purchase, a wedding, a promotion, or random timing. If analysts select customers precisely because their observed spending was extreme, the selected group contains many people who experienced unusually positive temporary factors. Those factors are unlikely to repeat for everyone, so the group’s next measurement tends to move closer to its long-run average. The same logic works at the low end. Some unusually inactive customers will become more active simply because the temporary factors that made them extreme disappear. Regression to the mean is not a claim that customers never change. It is a warning about before-and-after comparisons made after selecting extreme observations. A control group chosen under the same selection rule can help distinguish natural reversion from treatment effect. Random assignment after selection is particularly useful because both treatment and control groups are exposed to the same tendency to regress. Multiple historical periods can also help identify customers with persistently high or low behavior rather than one-period extremes. Analysts should separate absolute change from rank migration as well. A customer can leave the top decile even while spending increases if other customers increase more. Conversely, the top group can remain the same while the whole market declines. Shrinkage and hierarchical models formalize the idea that extreme noisy estimates should often be pulled toward a population average when predicting future behavior. In communication, “last year’s top customers spent less this year” is a valid descriptive statement. “Our best customers are losing loyalty” requires additional evidence. Whenever a group is selected because it was exceptional, analysts should ask how much movement toward normal would be expected even without an intervention. Analysts should define the population, observation window, and decision rule before interpreting the result. A useful review separates the observed pattern from the mechanism that may have produced it and from the action that should follow. paragraphs.zh: 繁中完整翻譯與解說：本文重點在於把 model metric 或 KPI 放回實際 decision context。數字變大不一定更好；極端群體可能自然回歸平均；ranking 與 probability calibration 是不同能力；歷史資料也會承載舊政策；而 campaign 真正關心的常常是 intervention 所創造的增量效果。
paragraphs.ja: 日本語完全訳・解説：model metricやKPIはdecision contextの中で解釈する必要がある。数値が大きいこと自体が良いとは限らず、極端群は平均へ回帰し、rankingとprobability calibrationは別の性能である。historical dataには旧policyも刻まれ、campaignではinterventionによる増分効果が重要になる。
